evidence: Cic. Att. 4.11.2: cum homine mīrificō … Dionȳsiō
Traupman 147, 152: mīrifica est, she is fantastic
terms.comment: The warm word of Cicero’s letters, of people and things alike; the adverb mīrificē, wonderfully, is even commoner there. Literally “causing wonder”, so it can also mean strange, extraordinary (Lewis & Short).
Very bright, so splendid, noble, famous; praise of a deed, a speech, a book (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Traupman 146, 159: exemplum admīrābile, a wonderful example
terms.comment: Worth admiring; Cicero also uses it in irony: ō admīrābilem impudentiam! (Cic. Phil. 3.18, Lewis & Short).
Above all in mīrābile dictū, wonderful to tell; of anything that causes wonder, pleasant or not.

phrases.latin: nōs hīc vorāmus litterās cum homine mīrificō (ita mē hercule sentiō) Dionȳsiō
phrases.english: here we are devouring books with Dionysius, a wonderful man (I really mean it)

phrases.latin: tuumque simul prōmptum animum et alacrem perspexī ad dēfendendam rem pūblicam mīrificamque cēpī voluptātem ex hāc tuā dīligentiā
phrases.english: and I saw how ready and eager you are to defend the state, and your care gave me wonderful pleasure

phrases.latin: dictū mīrābile, tenuit nōn sōlum āles captam semel sēdem
phrases.english: wonderful to tell, the bird not only kept the seat it had once taken
